subtitulo: English turns up often and this course will not promise you it always will — because speaking is the weakest of the four skills in the index, and six Greek words carry the rest
cena: You opened at the counter in English, the answer came back in one careful word, and now neither of you is sure which language this exchange is in.
frasePiso: Six words first, then the request. And when the ear runs out, ask for a pen.

fatosDatados.afirmacao: The EF English Proficiency Index 2025 places Greece at 592, ranked twentieth globally, in the «High» band, down ten points on the previous edition. Broken down by skill: reading 600, listening 592, writing 571 and speaking 533 — speaking is the weakest of the four. The caveat is obligatory and EF states it itself: respondents are self-selected, have internet access, and are skewed towards people already interested in languages. The index therefore does not measure the English of the Greek population; it measures the English of Greeks who chose to sit an online test. It supports saying that Greece figures among the high-proficiency countries in commercial self-selected indices, and never supports any claim of the form «X per cent of Greeks speak English».
fatosDatados.fonte: EF English Proficiency Index 2025 — Grécia 592, #20 global, banda «High»; por habilidade: leitura 600, compreensão oral 592, escrita 571, fala 533. Ressalva de autosseleção admitida pela própria EF

fatosDatados.afirmacao: The romanisation you meet on Greek road signs is a standard: ΕΛΟΤ 743, second edition of 2001, identical to ISO 843:1997, adopted by the British PCGN in 1996 and recommended by the United Nations in resolution V/19 of 1987. The PCGN's Greece Toponymic Factfile of April 2020 records verbatim that ELOT 743 «is very widely used on road signs in Greece as well as printed guide books», and also that it «is a less reliable guide to Modern Greek pronunciation» than the BGN/PCGN system of 1962 that it replaced. Reading the Latin-letter version of a Greek word aloud therefore does not produce the Greek pronunciation of it.
fatosDatados.fonte: PCGN, «Greece Toponymic Factfile», abril 2020; ΕΛΟΤ 743, 2ª edição, 2001 (= ISO 843:1997); resolução ONU V/19 (1987)

steps.pt: You will meet English here, often. What this part will not do is promise you that you always will.
The commercial index puts Greece at 592 for 2025, twentieth in the world, in the High band.
With one caveat the publisher states itself: people opt into that test online. It measures them, not a country.
The useful detail is inside it. Reading scores 600 and speaking 533 — speaking is the weakest of the four.
So the person in front of you may read your English better than they can answer it. Write things down.

steps.acao: He has offered you a language and told you its size in the same breath. Slow down and shorten your sentences.
steps.pt: Yes, I speak a little English. A little!
Six words carry almost every counter in the country, and you already know most of them.
Καλημέρα, καλησπέρα, γεια σας, παρακαλώ, ευχαριστώ, συγγνώμη. That is the whole set.

steps.promptPt: Half past nine, the bakery door, a woman already looking up at you. Put the greeting in before anything else. Speak now.
steps.pt: Good morning.

steps.promptPt: What you need next is too complicated for the Greek you have. Ask before you launch into it, and open politely. Speak now.
steps.pt: Excuse me, do you speak English?
Παρακαλώ does three jobs on its own: please, you're welcome, and go ahead. Listen for which one.

steps.acao: Same word, third job. Said like a question it means go ahead, or say that again.
steps.pt: Sorry — go ahead?

steps.promptPt: She answered you in fast Greek because your greeting was good. Set the level honestly, in her language. Speak now.
steps.pt: Greek — only a little.

steps.promptPt: The answer came at full speed and you caught two words of it. Ask for the same sentence at a different pace. Speak now.
steps.pt: Slower, please.

steps.promptPt: It is a platform number and a time, and your ear has now failed twice. Move the problem onto paper. Speak now.
steps.pt: Can you write it down?

steps.acao: He is offering you Latin letters to help. Take them for the meaning, not for the sound.
steps.es: Να σου το γράψω και στα λατινικά, να το διαβάσεις.
steps.pt: I'll write it in Latin letters too, so you can read it.
steps.tts: Να σου το γράψω και στα λατινικά, να το διαβάσεις.

steps.pt: The greeting changes in the middle of the day, and nobody agrees on exactly when it does.
Between noon and five you will hear all three, from natives, hesitating. Καλό μεσημέρι covers the gap.

steps.acao: That hesitation is real and it is hers, not yours. Whichever you picked was fine.
steps.es: Καλησπέρα! Ή καλημέρα ακόμα; Ούτε εγώ ξέρω.
steps.pt: Good evening! Or is it still good morning? I don't know either.
steps.tts: Καλησπέρα! Ή καλημέρα ακόμα; Ούτε εγώ ξέρω.

steps.promptPt: It is six in the evening and the same door, the same woman, the second visit of the day. Greet her for the hour it now is. Speak now.
steps.pt: Good evening.
Signs give you Greek in Latin letters, by a standard, and that version is a poor guide to how a word sounds.
So ask for the Greek word and copy the stress off a voice, never off a road sign.

steps.promptPt: You are holding the thing and you have no word for it in either language. Point, and ask for the local one. Speak now.
steps.es: Πώς το λένε αυτό στα ελληνικά;
steps.pinyin: POS to LE-ne af-TO sta e-li-ni-KA
steps.pt: What's this called in Greek?
steps.tts: Πώς το λένε αυτό στα ελληνικά;

steps.acao: You have the word and the stress in one go. Say it straight back before it fades.
steps.pt: This? Slowly now — and the stress is near the end: ko-lo-ki-tho-ke-FTE-dhes.

steps.promptPt: She spent four minutes on a two-minute customer. Close it with the two words that always belong at a door. Speak now.
steps.pt: Thank you very much. Goodbye!

steps.es: Καλημέρα σας. Συγγνώμη, μιλάτε αγγλικά; Ευχαριστώ πολύ. Γεια σας!
steps.pinyin: ka-li-ME-ra sas · si-GHNO-mi, mi-LA-te ang-li-KA · ef-ha-ri-STO po-LI · YA sas
steps.pt: Shadow the opening and the closing. Everything else in the exchange fits between them.
steps.tts: Καλημέρα σας. Συγγνώμη, μιλάτε αγγλικά; Ευχαριστώ πολύ. Γεια σας!

steps.pt: A05 done. Six words, one honest caveat about the index, and a pen for whatever the ear misses.

aprofundar.titulo: What the number can say, and the six words that do the work

secoes.titulo: What the index measures, and what it does not
secoes.corpo: The EF English Proficiency Index 2025 puts Greece at 592, twentieth globally, in the band it calls High, ten points down on the previous edition. EF states the limitation itself: respondents are self-selected, they need internet access, and they skew towards people already interested in languages. So the index does not measure the English of the Greek population — it measures the English of Greeks who decided to sit an online test. That is worth saying plainly, because the number gets quoted as though it were a census. This course will tell you that Greece figures among the high-proficiency countries in commercial self-selected indices. It will not tell you what proportion of people you meet will speak English, because no material in this research supports such a figure.

exemplos.pt: Excuse me, do you speak English?

secoes.titulo: The asymmetry inside the number, which is the actionable part
secoes.corpo: The skill breakdown is where the practical instruction lives: reading 600, listening 592, writing 571, speaking 533. Speaking is the weakest of the four by a clear margin. Translated into a counter, that means the person in front of you may follow your English comfortably and still find answering it hard work — and it means the gap between what they understand and what they will volunteer is wider than you would guess from the first exchange. Two habits follow. Shorten your sentences and slow the delivery rather than raising the volume. And when the exchange contains a number, a time, a platform or a street, move it onto paper: μπορείτε να το γράψετε; costs four words and removes the skill that scores lowest from the problem entirely.

Καλημέρα, καλησπέρα, γεια σας, παρακαλώ, ευχαριστώ, συγγνώμη. That is the entire courtesy kit and it covers nearly every counter you will stand at. Two of them do more than one job. Παρακαλώ is please, you're welcome and go ahead all at once, so you will hear it answering your thanks as often as you say it asking for something, and as a question it means say that again. Γεια σας is the polite form to a stranger or to more than one person, γεια σου the familiar one, and if you are not sure which, the plural is never wrong. What none of this comes with is a promised effect: nobody has studied what a well-pronounced ευχαριστώ actually buys, and this course does not claim a number for it. What can be said is smaller and truer — the words are short, you will hear all six back at you within a day, and using them puts you inside the exchange rather than beside it.

secoes.titulo: Midday, and the greeting nobody agrees about
secoes.corpo: The switch from καλημέρα to καλησπέρα has no normative source. There is a well-known prescriptive position — the lexicographer Babiniotis argues that the εσπέρα begins at sunset and that καλησπέρα at noon is imitation of a foreign habit — and there is ordinary practice, in which three different usages coexist quite happily. Between about noon and five you will hear natives hesitate, correct themselves and laugh about it, and καλό μεσημέρι exists precisely for that stretch. The honest teaching is that the ambiguity is real and shared. You cannot get this wrong in a way anybody notices, because the person opposite is not sure either.

secoes.titulo: The Latin-letter version is a different language of the same word
secoes.corpo: The romanisation on road signs is a standard — ΕΛΟΤ 743, second edition 2001, identical to ISO 843:1997, adopted by the PCGN in 1996 and recommended by the UN in 1987 — and the PCGN's own Greece factfile of April 2020 records both that it is very widely used on Greek road signs and printed guides, and that it is a less reliable guide to Modern Greek pronunciation than the older system it replaced. That is the whole warning: the Latin spelling is built to be converted back into Greek letters, not to be read aloud by an English speaker. Use it to match a word on a sign to a word on your ticket. For the sound, ask a person — πώς το λένε αυτό στα ελληνικά; — and copy the stress off the voice, because the accent mark on a Greek word of two syllables or more tells you exactly where it goes.

permissao: You are allowed to mangle ευχαριστώ. No study has ever measured what a good one buys or a bad one costs, so nobody can honestly sell you the effect — what is true is smaller and more useful: the word is short, you will hear it come back at you within a day, and the version you attempt is the one you will be corrected into. You are also allowed to ask for English outright, in Greek, after the greeting. That order is the whole trick, and it costs three seconds.
espelho: Anyone who has been served in their own country by somebody working in a second language knows both halves of this from the other side: how much they understood, and how much less they were willing to say out loud. That gap is the one you are standing in front of, and it is nobody's fault.

fichasCulturais.sinal: You ask a question in English, get a fluent-sounding start, and then the answer shrinks to two or three words and stops.
fichasCulturais.suaLeitura: They do not want to help me, or they have decided the conversation is over.
fichasCulturais.oQueEAli: In the EF index for 2025 Greece scores 600 on reading and 533 on speaking, the lowest of the four skills. The gap between understanding your question and producing an answer for it is real and measured — with the standing caveat that the index samples self-selected online test-takers rather than the population.
fichasCulturais.oQueVoceFaz: Shorten your sentences instead of repeating the long one, and put anything numerical onto paper: μπορείτε να το γράψετε; Give a beat of silence rather than filling it, because the answer is usually being assembled.
fichasCulturais.oQueMelhora: You get the platform number and the time instead of a shrug, and the exchange stops feeling like a refusal when it was only a harder task than you realised.
fichasCulturais.ondeNaoVale: Not a rule about anybody in particular. You will also meet people whose English is faster than yours and who would rather use it than watch you struggle — the index is a national average of volunteers, and it predicts nothing at all about the individual at the till.

fichasCulturais.sinal: At half past one you say καλημέρα, and the person answering seems to hesitate over which greeting to give you back.
fichasCulturais.suaLeitura: I used the wrong one and they are too polite to correct me.
fichasCulturais.oQueEAli: There is no norm to be wrong about. No normative source fixes the switch from καλημέρα to καλησπέρα; there is a named prescriptive position holding that the evening begins at sunset, and there is ordinary practice, where three usages coexist. Between noon and about five, natives hesitate too, which is why καλό μεσημέρι exists for the gap.
fichasCulturais.oQueVoceFaz: Pick either and carry on. If you want the safe one for the awkward hours, καλό μεσημέρι fits, and copying whichever greeting you were given is never wrong.
fichasCulturais.oQueMelhora: You stop rehearsing a clock rule that does not exist, and you spend the attention on the request instead of on the greeting.
fichasCulturais.ondeNaoVale: Not true at the edges of the day. At eight in the morning καλησπέρα is genuinely odd, and at ten at night so is καλημέρα — the ambiguity lives in the middle of the day, not across all of it.
